**ABSTRACT**

This study presents the design, development, and developer-side testing of the UNC Translator, an NLP-based Bikol-Naga to English translation system for the English Immersive Environment (EIE) Program of the University of Nueva Caceres. Students who speak Bikol-Naga as a first language may need to find an English word or phrase in the middle of a conversation, and no dedicated tool for Bikol-Naga to English translation within an academic English-immersion setting was identified in the literature reviewed. The system is a web application (Flask, SQLite, and a React interface) that translates typed or voice-dictated Bikol-Naga words, phrases, and sentences into English. Because large parallel corpora are not available for Bikol-Naga, it uses a lookup-first, rule-based hybrid rather than a neural model: a whole-input match against the researchers' dataset of 2,049 dictionary terms and 3,786 sentence pairs; example-based adaptation of a similar stored sentence; sentence construction from Bikol grammar rules taken from Mintz's Bikol Dictionary and Epstein's Standard Bikol; and a word-by-word fallback that marks unrecognized words. Each result is labeled with how it was produced, and grammar-built results show the rules and sources used. The system has three roles: Student and Teacher/Facilitator, who have identical access to translation and their own history, and Administrator, who manages accounts and reads the audit log. Passwords are stored as scrypt hashes, and the system applies per-account lockout, generic login errors, forced change of temporary passwords, and an audit log. In developer-side measurements on the researchers' own dataset, the grammar module alone built a sentence for 20.6% of the 3,786 sentence pairs with a mean word-overlap F1 of 0.68 against the researchers' English, and an automated suite of 42 tests passed. These are word-overlap figures, not BLEU scores or human judgments. Human validation of translation quality, the student and facilitator survey, and the user acceptance testing have not yet been carried out; their iii results are to be added. (DIPA PO SYA TOTALLY COMPLETED). The study contributes a documented, reusable Bikol-Naga resource and a working reference tool, and identifies the grammar structures that remain unsupported. Keywords: Bikol-Naga, Central Bikol, machine translation, rule-based translation, example-based translation, low-resource languages, English Immersive Environment

 **CHAPTER 1**  
**INTRODUCTION**  
This chapter presents the background and foundation of the study. It discusses the domain and context of the project, the setting where the research was conducted, and the rationale behind developing an NLP-based Bikol-Naga to English translation system for the English Immersive Environment (EIE) Program of the University of Nueva Caceres (UNC). It further presents the statement of the problem, the objectives of the study, the purpose and description of the system, its scope and delimitations, its limitations, and the definition of terms used throughout the study. 

**Project Context**  
          The Philippines recognizes two official languages, Filipino and English. Machine translation research on Philippine languages has covered several language pairs, including Filipino/Tagalog, Cebuano, Kankanaey, Maranao, Hiligaynon, and Ilocano; among these, a 2018 survey of Philippine machine translation work lists three projects for Ilocano but only one project each for Bikol, Cebuano, Kankanaey, Maranao, and Hiligaynon \[1\]. The University of Nueva Caceres implements an English Immersive Environment (EIE) Program, an institutional policy that requires students to communicate in English within the campus; a related emphasis on English immersion is reflected in the university's own Senior High School program page, which describes its learning environment as "technology enabled, english immersive, and industry milieu" \[2\]. While this policy is intended to strengthen the communicative competence of UNC students in preparation for professional and global engagement, its enforcement brings students' first languages into play. UNC is located in Naga City, where Central Bikol, locally known as Bikol-Naga, is spoken, and this study is premised on the observation that a number of UNC students speak Bikol-Naga as their first language. The proportion of such students is not established in this manuscript; it is documented from the respondent profile collected through the study's survey questionnaire (see Chapter 3). In effect, the EIE Program places students in a multi-language instructional environment: classroom instruction, requirements, and everyday campus communication are expected to take place in English, while the language that Bikol-Naga speaking students naturally think and reason in remains Bikol-Naga, so the two languages are constantly in play side by side rather than one simply replacing the other.  
A recent review of English language education policy in the Philippines points to several interlocking problems: inconsistent implementation of national language policies, not enough properly prepared English teachers to go around, and a school curriculum still weighted toward analyzing literature instead of building practical language skills; together, these are cited as reasons why many Filipino learners' English competency continues to fall short \[3\]. For students whose first language is Bikol-Naga, the shift demanded by an English-only campus policy may involve vocabulary access in addition to grammar: a student who instinctively thinks and reacts in Bikol-Naga may need to find the equivalent English word or phrase before speaking, which could lead to hesitation or a return to the mother tongue, particularly in informal, unplanned classroom or hallway interactions where no teacher or dictionary is on hand. This is the researchers' working assumption and is examined through the data gathering described in Chapter 3\. The one Bikol project identified in the 2018 survey mentioned above is a bi-directional Bikol-English statistical machine translator, built to assist non-linguists in translating survey questions, as reported in that survey \[1\]. A more recent transfer-based Bicolano-Tagalog translator \[4\] targets a different language pair and use case. Neither system was designed for, or evaluated within, an academic English-immersion setting, and neither targets Bikol-Naga (Central Bikol) specifically for the purpose of assisting students in complying with a campus-wide English policy. This leaves a concrete, addressable gap: as far as the researchers could determine, UNC students under the EIE Program currently have no dedicated, instant reference tool that converts the Bikol-Naga words and expressions they already think in into the English equivalents the policy requires them to use.   
             This study is anchored on that gap. It proposes the design and development of an NLP-based Bikol-Naga to English translation system intended specifically to support UNC students, faculty, and EIE Program facilitators by providing fast translation, by typing or by voice dictation, of common Bikol-Naga words, phrases, and sentences into English, drawing on approaches used in comparable studies on low-resource Philippine language pairs \[1, 4, 5\]. 

**Research Locale**  
           This study will be conducted at the University of Nueva Caceres (UNC), a private, nonsectarian higher education institution located along J. Hernandez Avenue, City of Naga, Camarines Sur, in the Bicol Region of the Philippines. Naga City is located in the Bicol Region, where Bikol-Naga (Central Bikol) is spoken, which makes UNC an appropriate locale for a study concerned with the use of Bikol-Naga among students who speak it. UNC is also the institution that implements the English Immersive Environment Program, the specific institutional policy this study seeks to support, which makes the university not only the site of data gathering but also the direct beneficiary community of the proposed system. Respondents and data sources for this study, including EIE Program coordinators, faculty facilitators, and students subject to the policy, will be drawn from within the UNC community.   
**Rationale**  
         The researchers' own experience as UNC students under the EIE Program suggests that keeping to English can be difficult in the middle of a live conversation, particularly when a student cannot immediately recall the English equivalent of a BikolNaga word. This is a working premise of the study and not a finding: the interviews and survey described in Chapter 3 are meant to examine whether, and in which situations, vocabulary difficulty affects students' use of English under the policy. Google Translate, a general-purpose translation tool, added Bikol to its supported languages on June 27, 2024 \[6\]; its listing names the language only as "Bikol" without specifying a variety, and, as far as the researchers could determine, general-purpose tools of this kind were not designed for the specific, real-time classroom-and-hallway use case this study addresses, and the few Bikol-related translation projects that do exist were likewise not built with this use case in mind. The researchers therefore saw an opportunity to design a purpose-built, lightweight NLP translation tool that a UNC student could consult in the moment a BikolNaga word or sentence comes to mind, in order to find its English equivalent and continue the conversation in English, thereby supporting rather than penalizing the student's compliance with the EIE Program. 

**Statement of the Problem**  
          This study, in general, seeks to design and develop an NLP-based translation system capable of accurately converting Bikol-Naga words, phrases, and simple to moderately complex sentences into their English equivalents, in order to assist University of Nueva Caceres students, faculty, and facilitators in complying with the requirements of the English Immersive Environment (EIE) Program. 

Specifically, this study seeks to answer the following questions: 

1\. What functional features and modules must the proposed system possess to provide timely and relevant Bikol-Naga to English translation support to students, faculty, and facilitators within the context of the EIE Program? 

2\. Which Natural Language Processing technique and translation approach best meet the selection criteria (fit with the size and coverage of the compiled Bikol-Naga corpus, translation accuracy, response time, and feasibility of implementation) for translating common campus-related vocabulary from Bikol-Naga to English, given the limited size of existing digital Bikol-Naga language resources?  

3\. To what extent does the developed system perform in terms of translation accuracy and in terms of usability and acceptability among its intended UNC users?  

**Objective of the Study**  
This study generally aims to design, develop, and evaluate an NLP-based BikolNaga to English translation system that supports the University of Nueva Caceres' English Immersive Environment Program by providing students, faculty, and facilitators with a fast and reliable reference for converting common Bikol-Naga words and expressions into English. 

Specifically, this study aims to: 

1\. Identify and implement the functional features and modules the system must possess, namely a login module, a translation engine module, a mic (voice input) module, a translation history module, a user administration module, and an audit log module, to provide timely and relevant translation support to EIE Program stakeholders. 

2\. . Select, using the criteria stated in Chapter 3 (Technique Selection), and implement a Natural Language Processing technique and translation approach for a lowresource language pair, capable of translating common Bikol-Naga campus vocabulary and sentences into English. The technique selected, a lookup-first rulebased hybrid, and its configuration are reported in Chapter 4\. 

3\. Evaluate the developed system's translation accuracy and assess its usability and acceptability through user acceptance testing involving UNC students, faculty, and EIE Program facilitators. 

**Purpose and Description**	  
The purpose of this study is to reduce the language-access barrier that Bikol-Naga speaking students of UNC may experience while complying with the English Immersive  Environment Program, by giving them an instant, purpose-built reference for the English equivalents of the Bikol-Naga words and expressions they naturally think in. Unlike general-purpose translation applications, which cover many languages broadly, the system is scoped narrowly to the vocabulary and everyday expressions relevant to campus life, making it directly usable within the specific context the EIE Program creates. This study does not test or compare general-purpose tools against the proposed system, and it makes no claim about how well those tools handle Bikol. The system, titled "UNC Translator," is a unidirectional Bikol-Naga to English translation application accessed through a web browser. Users log in with an account created by the system administrator, then type a Bikol-Naga word, phrase, or sentence, or dictate it by voice using the mic button. The translation engine looks the input up in a Bikol-Naga to English parallel corpus and dictionary compiled by the researchers; if the whole input is not found, it adapts a similar stored sentence, builds the sentence from Bikol grammar rules when every word is understood, or translates word by word and marks the words it could not translate. Every result shows how it was produced, so that the user knows how far to rely on it. The translation is saved to the user's translation history, which the user may archive and restore but which the system never deletes. The system supports three roles. Student and Teacher/Facilitator have identical access to translation and to their own history. Administrator creates accounts, assigns roles, resets passwords, deactivates and reactivates accounts, and reads the audit log, and does not translate or see any user's history.    
   
The following stakeholders are expected to benefit from the development and eventual deployment of this system: 

1\. UNC Students under the EIE Program. Students gain immediate access to English equivalents of Bikol-Naga words and expressions during classroom discussions, group work, and everyday campus interactions, which is intended to help reduce hesitation and support compliance with the English-only policy. 

2\. EIE Program Faculty and Facilitators. Faculty members and program facilitators gain a supplementary tool they can recommend or demonstrate to students who are struggling with the transition to English, which is intended to support the program without adding to their own workload. 

3\. System Administrator. The administrator can create and manage accounts and review security-relevant events without access to what users translate. 

4\. Future Researchers. The parallel corpus, the documented grammar rules, and the translation modules produced by this study are intended to contribute a reusable, documented language resource to the still-limited body of published Bikol-Naga NLP work, providing a foundation that future studies on Bikol-Naga or related Bikol dialects can build upon \[1\].  

**Scope and Delimitations**  
This study is limited to the design, development, and evaluation of a unidirectional Bikol-Naga to English translation system; translation from English back into Bikol-Naga is explicitly outside the scope of this project, as the EIE Program's requirement runs in one direction only, that is, from the students' native language into English. The system covers Central Bikol (Bikol-Naga) as spoken in Naga City and its immediate surrounding areas, and does not extend to other Bikol varieties, such as Rinconada Bikol, a distinct variety documented in its own dedicated text corpus study \[7\].   
The system accepts typed text input of up to 200 characters and also provides an optional voice dictation feature that lets a user speak the Bikol-Naga word, phrase, or sentence instead of typing it, using the browser's built-in speech-to-text capability to convert speech into text before it is handed to the translation engine. Building a dedicated Bikol-Naga speech recognition model is outside the scope of this study, as automatic speech recognition for Bikol has been pursued as a separate research effort in its own right \[8\]; the system therefore relies on existing, general-purpose speech-to-text support, and recognition accuracy for spoken Bikol-Naga is not guaranteed. The translation coverage is limited to common conversational and academic-context vocabulary and to the sentence structures that the grammar module supports; highly technical, literary, or figurative Bikol-Naga expressions are not guaranteed to be covered.   
Beyond the core translation function, the scope includes a personal translation history that the user may archive and restore, and an account system with three roles, Student, Teacher/Facilitator, and Administrator. The administrator functions include creating accounts, assigning roles, resetting passwords, deactivating and reactivating accounts, and viewing the audit log. Accounts are created only by the administrator; selfregistration and password recovery by e-mail are not provided. These supporting features are treated as standard application functionality built around the core translation engine, and are not themselves NLP research contributions of this study.   
The system is a web-based application written in Python with the Flask framework \[17\], a SQLite relational database \[18\] for the dictionary, corpus, accounts, history, and audit log, and a browser interface built with React \[19\]. The translation engine does not use a neural model or any external translation service; it combines dictionary and corpus lookup, example-based adaptation \[16\], and grammar rules drawn from Mintz \[14\] and Epstein \[15\]. The technique was selected during development against the criteria in Chapter 3, guided by the size and coverage of the corpus the researchers compiled and by comparable Philippine-language MT projects that worked within similar resource constraints \[1, 4, 5\]. 

**Limitations of the Study**  
The accuracy of the system is directly constrained by the size and coverage of the Bikol-Naga to English parallel corpus and dictionary that the researchers were able to compile within the project timeline; words, phrases, or sentence patterns not represented in this corpus may be translated incorrectly or not at all. Of the rows read from the researchers' dataset, 532 were not loaded because they need review (for example, the same Bikol text with different English, or entries that could not be split into columns), and 357 loaded terms carry more than one English entry, of which the first is shown as the primary translation, so some stored translations may need correction by a Bikol speaker. The system's understanding of context is limited, so idiomatic expressions, humor, and figures of speech specific to Bikol-Naga oral culture may not be translated with their intended meaning.   
The grammar module builds a sentence only when every word is understood and the sentence fits a supported pattern. Questions with the supported question words, equational sentences, existential sentences (may, igwa, mayo'), desire sentences with gusto, and verbal sentences with the actor-focus verb prefixes are supported; comparison, ability (maka-), and the \-on, \-an, and i- verb voices are not yet supported, and a sentence that uses them falls back to a rough word-by-word result. The grammar rules were taken from two published sources, and the English wording of inflected forms follows standard English morphology; a grammar-built sentence has not been validated by a Bikol speaker and must be checked by one. Any accuracy results reported by this study apply only to the corpus and test set used. Because the study focuses on the standard Bikol-Naga variety spoken in Naga City, users who speak a markedly different Bikol sub-variety or who frequently code-switch between Bikol-Naga, Filipino, and English within a single sentence may experience reduced translation accuracy.   
The optional voice dictation feature relies on the browser's general-purpose speech-to-text support rather than a Bikol-Naga-specific speech recognition model; its accuracy in transcribing spoken Bikol-Naga cannot be guaranteed and may introduce additional errors upstream of the translation engine itself, and the feature has not been tested by the researchers. On security, the password hashing uses scrypt with the default parameters of the Werkzeug library, which are below the minimum cost parameter that the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet recommends for scrypt \[23\], and the minimum password length is set to 8 characters for the demonstration version, which is shorter than the 15 characters OWASP recommends for accounts without multi-factor authentication \[22\]; both should be hardened before any wider deployment. The responsetime figures reported in Chapter 4 were measured by the researchers in a test environment and not on the pilot server. Finally, as with any corpus-driven translation approach, translation quality is expected to improve as more corpus data is added over time, meaning the version evaluated in this study represents an initial, rather than final, level of accuracy. 

**Definition of Terms**

1. Natural Language Processing (NLP). A field of artificial intelligence concerned with enabling computers to process, analyze, and generate human language; in this study, NLP refers specifically to the techniques used to analyze Bikol-Naga input text and produce an English translation.   
2. Machine Translation (MT). The use of software to translate text from one natural language to another without human intervention; in this study, MT refers to the automated conversion of Bikol-Naga text into English.   
3. Bikol-Naga (Central Bikol). The Bikol dialect spoken predominantly in Naga City and the surrounding areas of Camarines Sur; in this study, it refers to the source language of the translation system.   
4. English Immersive Environment (EIE) Program. The University of Nueva Caceres' institutional policy requiring students to use English as the primary language of communication within the campus.   
5. Parallel Corpus. A collection of texts in one language aligned with their translations in another language; in this study, it refers to the Bikol-Naga to English sentence pairs compiled by the researchers and stored in the database.   
6. Dictionary/Lookup Module. The component of the system that stores and retrieves the compiled Bikol-Naga to English word entries used to produce a translation.   
   7\. Rule-Based Translation. Translation that applies hand-written grammar rules and a bilingual dictionary; in this study, the grammar module that builds an English sentence from Bikol-Naga words.   
   8\. Example-Based Translation (adaptation). Translation that reuses the stored English of a similar sentence and swaps the words that differ using the dictionary; in this study, an adapted result changes at most two words of a stored sentence and is marked for the user.   
   9\. Grammar-Built Sentence. A translation produced by the grammar module and not found as a whole in the dataset; it is labeled as such and lists the rules and sources used.   
   10\. Role-Based Access Control. Limiting what a user can do according to the role of the account; in this study, the Student, Teacher/Facilitator, and Administrator roles.   
   11\. Hashed Password. A password stored only as the output of a one-way function (scrypt in this study), so that the original password is not kept.   
   12\. Audit Log. A record of security-relevant events, such as sign-ins and account changes, with the time, the user who acted, and the account affected.   
   13\. Word-Overlap F1. A score between 0 and 1 that compares the words of the system's English with the words of the researchers' English for the same sentence; it is not a BLEU score and not a human judgment of quality.   
   

CHAPTER 2  
**REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE**  
This chapter presents the technical background necessary to understand the system, followed by a review of related literature, studies, and existing systems concerning machine translation for Philippine languages, particularly Bikol dialects, and the challenges surrounding the University of Nueva Caceres' English Immersive Environment Program. The chapter closes with a synthesis explaining how the study relates to, and differs from, the works reviewed. 

**Technical Background**  
  Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the branch of artificial intelligence concerned with enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language. Machine Translation (MT), a core NLP application, is the automatic transformation of text from a source language into a target language. Three broad families of MT approach have been used historically: rule-based machine translation, which relies on linguist-authored grammar rules and bilingual dictionaries to transform source text; statistical machine translation (SMT), which derives translation probabilities from a bilingual parallel corpus rather than hand-written rules; and neural machine translation (NMT), which uses trained neural networks and, per a 2021 survey of neural machine translation for low-resource languages, still performs suboptimally on low-resource language pairs compared to high-resource ones due to the unavailability of large parallel corpora \[9\]. Low-resource languages, meaning languages for which little digitized parallel text is publicly available, pose a particular challenge for NMT for this reason. The Bikol translation studies reviewed in this chapter used statistical \[1\], transfer-based \[4\], and rulebased \[10\] approaches rather than NMT. Philippine languages, including Bikol, fall into this low-resource category: a 2018 survey of Philippine machine translation work lists three projects for Ilocano but only one project each for Bikol, Cebuano, Kankanaey, Maranao, and Hiligaynon \[1\].   
                Philippine languages also present specific linguistic challenges for translation regardless of the approach chosen. Verbs have both tense and focus \[1\]. The introduction to the Bikol dictionary of Mintz also describes affixes, tenses, plurals, markers, and pronouns for Bikol \[14\]. These structural features mean that a translation system for a Philippine language pair typically requires more than direct word-for-word substitution.   
                Example-based machine translation was introduced by Nagao as translation by analogy: instead of analyzing a whole sentence with grammar rules, the system finds similar sentence pairs in a collection of bilingual examples, reuses their translations, and substitutes the parts that differ; Nagao used a thesaurus to judge which stored examples are closest \[16\]. This approach suits a small corpus because it needs no trained model, and the researchers use it in the system for inputs that differ from a stored sentence by one or two words.   
                  A rule-based approach needs a description of the source language. For BikolNaga, the researchers used two published descriptions: the Bikol Dictionary by Mintz, whose introduction, "Use of the Dictionary," describes the affixes, tenses, plurals, markers, and pronouns of the language \[14\], and Standard Bikol by Epstein, a language course text prepared for the Peace Corps \[15\]. According to these sources, Central Bikol marks the role of a noun phrase with small function words (an, si, nin, kan, ni, and sa), uses separate sets of pronouns for the subject and for the possessor or actor, and marks verb tense and focus with the affixes nag-, mag-, and ma- \[14\] and the infix \-in- \[14, 15\]. These structural features, together with the observation in Section 2.1 that verbs have both tense and focus \[1\], are the reason the system does more than substitute words one by one.   
                The system is built on common web technologies. Flask is a lightweight web framework for Python that handles the web requests, sessions, and cookies of the   
application \[17\]. SQLite is a self-contained relational database engine that stores its data in a single file \[18\], and the system accesses it from Python through the sqlite3 module. React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces \[19\], and the optional voice input uses the browser's Web Speech API for speech recognition \[20\]; support for that API varies between browsers, and a recognizer for Bikol-Naga is not part of it.   
                 Because the system holds user accounts, it follows published security guidance. The scrypt function, specified in RFC 7914, is a password-based key derivation function designed to be costly in memory so that large-scale password guessing is expensive \[21\]. The OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet recommends storing passwords only as salted hashes made with a function such as Argon2id or scrypt, with cost parameters set high enough \[23\]. The OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet addresses password length, generic error messages at login, and limiting repeated failed attempts \[22\], and the OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet identifies authentication events and account-management actions as events to record \[24\]. The handling of personal data in the system is also subject to the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173\) \[25\]. 

**Related Literatures & Studies**  
             Fernandez et al. developed a bi-directional Bikol-English statistical machine translator to assist non-linguists in translating survey questions, as reported in the survey by   
            Oco and Roxas \[1\]. This study directly informs the present project's decision to build a dedicated Bikol-Naga to English parallel corpus rather than relying on generalpurpose translation resources, though the present study narrows the scope to a single translation direction and to Bikol-Naga specifically, in support of a defined institutional use case.   
             Sagum proposed a transfer-based bi-directional machine translation system between Bicolano and Tagalog, using language resources such as dictionaries and rules   
together with statistical approaches, and reported evaluation scores of 74.75% for Tagalog to Bicolano and 71.7% for Bicolano to Tagalog translation \[4\]. The researchers accessed only the abstract of this paper, which does not state the evaluation metric or the corpus used. It is relevant to the present study as a Bikol-related system that relies on dictionaries and rules, although it translates between Bicolano and Tagalog and not into English. Because the present study targets informal, everyday campus speech, its corpus is planned around conversational, campus-relevant sources.   
                Velasco et al. built an offline mobile translation app for Tagalog-Bicol using a rulebased NLP approach with a linear search algorithm for dictionary-based translation retrieval, implemented in Python and developed under an Agile process; its evaluation combined NLP-based methods with human assessment by native speakers of translation quality, fluency, and contextual accuracy, together with usability testing \[10\]. This study is the closest match to the present proposal in both technology choices and evaluation approach, since it also uses a Python-based, dictionary-driven design together with human assessment by native speakers, which is consistent with the dictionary-driven design and the use of human assessment planned for the present system; it nonetheless targets Tagalog-Bicol rather than Bikol-Naga-English and is not built around the EIE Program use case.   
                Adlaon and Marcos documented the process of building a language resource for a Cebuano-Filipino neural machine translation system, including the use of biblical texts and web sources as parallel text, and the application of subword unit translation for verbs \[5\]. Although this work targets Cebuano rather than Bikol, its detailed treatment of parallelcorpus construction for a Philippine low-resource language pair offers a useful reference for the corpus-building phase of the present study.   
               Oñate and Pandes developed a Rinconada Bikol text corpus from Nabua and analyzed it using corpus linguistics techniques, and also trained a bag-of-words sentiment analyzer on 500 sentences labeled as positive, negative, or neutral \[7\]. While Rinconada Bikol is a different Bikol variety from Bikol-Naga and the study's task, sentiment analysis, differs from translation, the work shows that a text corpus for a Bikol variety can be built and analyzed, which supports the present study's plan to compile a dedicated Bikol-Naga corpus rather than assuming one already exists.   
               Liao et al. worked on automatic speech recognition for two Philippine languages, Bikol and Kapampangan \[8\]. This shows that speech recognition for Bikol has been studied as a separate research effort in its own right. For this reason, the present study does not attempt to build a custom Bikol-Naga speech recognizer; where the proposed system offers voice dictation as a convenience input option, it relies on existing generalpurpose speech-to-text support rather than a purpose-built Bikol-Naga acoustic model, and speech recognition accuracy is treated as a known limitation rather than a contribution of this study. Oco and Roxas surveyed Philippine machine translation work from 1998 to 2018\. They noted that in all the transfer-based projects the corpus size was limited and the vocabulary stayed within the available resources, and that most of the works they presented focused only on text \[1\]. The survey further confirmed that, as of 2018, Bikol had been the subject of only one identifiable published bi-directional Bikol-English MT project \[1\], underscoring how little dedicated Bikol translation research existed prior to this study.   
                   On the language-learning side of this study's domain, Kilag et al. reviewed the state of English Language Education policy in the Philippines and concluded that uneven policy implementation, a shortage of well-prepared English teachers, and a curriculum still leaning heavily on literary study rather than practical language skills have kept many Filipino students' English skills from advancing \[3\]. This literature gives national-level background on why English competency remains a challenge for many Filipino learners. It does not itself show how an English-immersion policy such as UNC's EIE Program affects students, which is what the interviews and survey of this study are meant to examine.   
                 Closer to the present study's own locale, Garganera et al. measured the English proficiency and communicative competence of graduate students at a graduate school in the Bicol Region using a standardized English proficiency test, and found that most of the 118 respondents were at an intermediate level of communicative competence, with doctoral candidates scoring higher than the other degree-level groups \[11\]. Conducted in the Bicol Region, the same region as the University of Nueva Caceres, this study provides local context on English proficiency, although its respondents were graduate students at one institution and its findings cannot be assumed to apply to UNC students. 

**Related Systems**  
	Google Translate, a general-purpose translation platform, added Bikol to its supported languages on June 27, 2024 \[6\]. The listing names the language only as "Bikol" without specifying a variety, so it is unclear whether it specifically reflects the Bikol-Naga (Central Bikol, Naga City) variety relevant to this study, and, as far as the researchers could determine, it is not designed for the real-time, classroom-and-hallway use case the EIE Program creates.   
            The transfer-based Bicolano-Tagalog system developed by Sagum is a Bikolrelated system that uses dictionaries and rules together with statistical approaches \[4\]. However, it translates between Bicolano and Tagalog rather than into English, and it was not built around a specific institutional use case such as an English-immersion policy, which is the specific gap the present study addresses.   
            The offline Tagalog-Bicol mobile translation app developed by Velasco et al. is closer still in overall system design, sharing a Python-based, dictionary-driven design and the use of human assessment by native speakers in its evaluation \[10\]; it differs from the present proposal in language pair, direction, and its offline mobile app format rather than an EIE Program-specific, browser-based system.   
            Two further resources are related to the system without being translation systems. The Bikol Dictionary by Mintz is a printed and, in an open-access edition, digital dictionary of Bikol with notes on the grammar of the language \[14\], and Standard Bikol by Epstein is a language course text \[15\]. Neither is software and neither translates a sentence; they are the reference works from which the grammar rules of the system were taken, so the system makes their content usable as a translation tool for students. 

**Synthesis**  
             Taken together, the reviewed literature points to two things. First, machine translation for Bikol has been attempted using statistical \[1\], transfer-based \[4\], and rulebased \[10\] methods despite limited corpus sizes, yet Bikol as a whole remains one of the least-studied Philippine language translation directions \[1\], and no published work identified through the search described below has produced a system translating specifically from Bikol-Naga into English for use within an academic English-immersion context. Second, the literature traces Filipino students' struggles with English competency to a mix of policy, staffing, and curricular issues \[3\], which provides national-level background for the study's interest in a supplementary tool of the kind proposed here.  
             Search strategy. The research gap stated above is a conclusion of the researchers' literature search and not a claim that no such work exists anywhere. The sources reviewed were located through web searches and through the survey by Oco and Roxas \[1\]; the records found are hosted by the ACL Anthology, ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Springer, and arXiv. The searches combined "Bikol" or "Bicolano" with "machine translation," with no date limit applied; the most recent searches were done in October 2026\. This was not a systematic review, so relevant unpublished, non-indexed, or inaccessible works may have been missed.    
             The present study is therefore not a duplication of any of the works reviewed. It differs from the Bikol-English statistical translator of Fernandez et al. (as reported in \[1\]) by narrowing the translation direction to Bikol-Naga-to-English only and by building its corpus around campus and classroom vocabulary rather than general usage. It differs from the transfer-based Bicolano-Tagalog system of Sagum \[4\] in both target language and intended use case. It differs from the offline Tagalog-Bicol app of Velasco et al. \[10\] in language pair and in being built specifically around the EIE Program rather than as a general-purpose offline tool. It differs from the Rinconada Bikol corpus work of Oñate and Pandes \[7\] in dialect, task, and application domain. Rather, this study extends the small but growing body of Bikol-focused NLP research identified in the survey by Oco and Roxas \[1\] into a new, previously unaddressed application: a Bikol-Naga to English translation tool purpose-built to support students, faculty, and facilitators of the University of Nueva Caceres' English Immersive Environment Program.   
               In terms of approach, the reviewed Bikol systems used statistical \[1\], transferbased \[4\], and rule-based \[10\] methods, and none of them is reported as example-based in the sources the researchers accessed. The system combines the dictionary-driven design of Velasco et al. \[10\] with example-based adaptation \[16\] and with grammar rules taken from published descriptions of Bikol \[14, 15\], and it labels each result with how it was produced. This combination, together with the institutional use case, is what distinguishes the present study from the works reviewed.   
CHAPTER 3  
**DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY**  
This chapter presents the research and development methodology followed in designing and building the NLP-Based Bikol-Naga to English Translation System. It covers the research methodology used to investigate the problem, the software development methodology used to build the system, the requirement analysis and specifications, the system design, and the testing and evaluation procedures. The interviews, the survey, and the user acceptance testing are written as planned procedures because they had not been carried out when this manuscript was prepared; the development of the system and the developer-side tests are written as done. 

**Research Methodology**  
![][image1]  
Figure 3.1: Conceptual Framework of Exploratory Research for the Development of the Proposed System   
The study follows an exploratory research design, appropriate given the limited amount of existing published work on Bikol machine translation \[1\]. As shown in the conceptual framework, the Domain Knowledge Requirements and User and System Requirements are drawn from the problems and gaps identified in the review of related literature, studies, and systems, together with information requirements to be gathered from EIE Program coordinators, faculty facilitators, and students. These requirements inform the System Design, Software Development (following the Feature-Driven Development methodology), and Software Testing activities that will produce the proposed system. In parallel, the Software Evaluation Criteria will be applied: Technique Selection during development, and the remaining criteria once the system is built, through the software testing and User Acceptance Testing described under Testing and Evaluation, with the resulting evaluation and feedback looping back to refine the corpus, requirements, and design in successive iterations, consistent with the exploratory and iterative nature of this research. 

***Data Collection Methods***  
	Key-Informant Interviews. The researchers will conduct structured interviews with EIE Program coordinators and faculty facilitators to identify the specific communication situations in which Bikol-Naga to English vocabulary gaps most frequently disrupt students' compliance with the English-only policy. These interviews will inform the list of common words, phrases, and sentence templates prioritized in the initial translation corpus.   
      Key-Informant Interview Procedure. Number and selection: the number of key informants will be set with the research adviser before the interviews and reported in the final manuscript. Informants are chosen through purposive sampling; each must be currently serving as an EIE Program coordinator or faculty facilitator at UNC and must agree to be interviewed. Mode and duration: the interviews will be held face-to-face at the university, or by video call if an informant cannot meet in person, and each is planned to last about 15 to 20 minutes; the actual mode and length of every interview will be recorded and reported in the final manuscript. Interview guide development: the guide will be written from the study's objectives and the problems identified in the review of related literature, and will be checked by the research adviser before use; the same seven open-ended questions will be asked of every informant.   
         Note-taking, consent, and confidentiality. The interviews will not be audiorecorded. Two researchers will take written notes during each interview, and the notes will be typed up by the researchers right after the interview, keeping answers given in BikolNaga in their original wording and adding an English translation only where needed for reporting. Before each interview, the informant will be given a consent statement that explains the purpose of the study, what will be asked, and that no audio recording will be made, and that the informant may skip any question or stop at any time. Informants will be identified in the typed notes and in the manuscript by codes (for example, KI-1) and not by name. The notes will be kept only by the research team and used only for this study, in line with the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173).   
       Survey Questionnaires. A survey questionnaire will be administered to UNC students who meet the inclusion criteria stated under Respondents and Sampling (students enrolled in programs covered by the EIE Program) to gather the specific BikolNaga words and expressions they most often find themselves needing to translate on the spot, as well as their expectations for how such a tool should be accessed and used. The questionnaire also includes a respondent-profile item on the student's first language, so that the number of Bikol-Naga speakers among the respondents is documented from the study's own data. Responses will be used both to prioritize corpus content and to define usability requirements for the system's interface. 

**Respondents and Sampling**   
            Two groups of participants are planned. The first group is the key informants: EIE Program coordinators and faculty facilitators of UNC. The second group is UNC students enrolled in programs covered by the EIE Program.   
             Sampling Technique. Key informants will be chosen through purposive sampling, since only people who are directly involved in implementing the EIE Program can describe how it works in practice. Students will be reached through convenience sampling, meaning students who meet the inclusion criteria below and are available and willing to take part. Because of this, the student responses describe the students who answered and cannot be assumed to represent all UNC students. The target number of key informants and student respondents will be set with the research adviser before data gathering, and the number who actually take part will be reported in the final manuscript.   
           Inclusion Criteria. Key informants must be currently serving as an EIE Program coordinator or faculty facilitator at UNC and must agree to be interviewed. Student respondents must be currently enrolled at UNC in a program covered by the EIE Program, must be able to read the questionnaire, and must give consent; students under 18 years old will take part only with the consent of a parent or guardian. Students are not required to speak Bikol-Naga in order to answer, because the questionnaire records each student's first language so that the number of Bikol-Naga speakers among the respondents is documented. Incomplete questionnaires will be excluded from the analysis.   
           Distribution and Response Rate. The questionnaire will be given to students as printed copies, handed out in person by the researchers, with the permission of the concerned teachers, to students who meet the inclusion criteria and agree to take part. The researchers will keep a count of the copies handed out and the copies returned. The response rate will be computed as the number of completed questionnaires divided by the number of questionnaires handed out, multiplied by 100, and will be reported in the final manuscript together with the number of incomplete questionnaires that were excluded. 

**Research Instruments Interview Protocol.**   
           Interview Protocol. The interviews are structured: the same written guide of seven open-ended questions will be used with every key informant. The questions cover the informant's role in the EIE Program; the situations in which students find it hard to keep to English; what students usually do when they cannot find the English word; the informant's own view of the reasons behind these difficulties; the words and expressions students most often need help with; the help currently available to students; and what the informant would want from, and worry about in, a Bikol-Naga to English translation tool. Informants answer in their own words, and the interviewer will not suggest answers. Written notes will be taken during each interview; the interviews will not be audio-recorded.    
        Questionnaire Construction. The student questionnaire is built from the study's objectives and the interview guide. It has a respondent profile (program, year level, first language, and whether the student speaks Bikol-Naga in daily life); five statements on English use on campus, answered on a five-point scale from Never to Always, on how often students try to use English, think of the Bikol-Naga word first, cannot think of the English word, switch to Bikol-Naga or Filipino when they do not know it, or stay silent; checklists of the situations in which this happens and of what students do when it happens; an optional item on other reasons it is hard to follow the English-only policy; an openended item on up to five Bikol-Naga words and expressions they most often need in English; and items on whether they have used a translation tool for Bikol-Naga before, how they would prefer to use a translation tool, on what device, and, as an optional item, what the tool should do to be useful to them. The items are worded neutrally so that the answers can either support or contradict the researchers' working premise.   
        Questionnaire Validation. Before it is distributed, the questionnaire and the interview guide will be reviewed by the research adviser for relevance to the objectives and for clarity of wording. The questionnaire will then be tried out with three to five students who will not be counted among the respondents, to check that the items are understood, and items will be revised based on their comments. No statistical reliability test is planned, because the questionnaire is meant to describe students' experiences and needs and is not a scale that measures a single trait.   
        The interview guide and the questionnaire are included as Appendix A. The questionnaire and interview guide are not yet attached they are to be added once finalized with the research adviser. HINDI PA PO SIYA NA FINALIZE KAYA DI PA NAMIN MAILAGAY.

**Ethical Considerations**   
Participation in the interviews and the survey is voluntary. Before answering or being interviewed, each participant will be given a consent statement that explains the purpose of the study, what will be asked, that questions may be skipped and participation may be stopped at any time, and how the answers will be used. The questionnaire does not ask for names, and interview notes use codes instead of names. The data will be kept only by the research team, used only for this study, and handled in line with the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173). Permission to conduct the interviews and the survey will be requested from the research adviser and the concerned UNC offices before data gathering begins. The questionnaire and the interview guide will be included as appendices so that the data collection can be reproduced and evaluated. 

***Data Analysis Techniques***  
         The data collected will be analyzed using the following techniques:   
        Descriptive Statistics. The questionnaire responses will be treated with descriptive statistics only. Frequency counts and percentages (percentage \= frequency divided by the number of respondents, multiplied by 100\) will be used for the respondent profile, including first language and daily use of Bikol-Naga, and for the checklist items on the situations in which students have trouble finding the English word, what they do when they cannot, whether they have used a translation tool before, how they would prefer to use a translation tool, and on what device. For the five-point items, the frequency of each answer and the mean (the sum of the ratings divided by the number of respondents) will be reported. The Bikol-Naga words and expressions that students list will be tallied and ranked from most to least frequently mentioned. No inferential test is planned, because the sample is chosen by convenience and the questionnaire is meant to describe students' experiences and needs, not to generalize to all UNC students. Microsoft Excel will be used to encode and tabulate the responses and to compute these statistics.   
       Thematic Analysis. Interview and open-ended survey responses will be grouped into recurring themes, such as classroom-discussion vocabulary, greetings and small talk, and campus-facility terms, in order to organize the corpus-building effort around the situations where students report the most difficulty.   
       Corpus Frequency Analysis. The compiled Bikol-Naga text samples will be analyzed for word and phrase frequency to prioritize which vocabulary items and sentence patterns to encode first into the system's dictionary and corpus, ensuring that the most commonly needed translations are supported before less frequent or specialized vocabulary. The word and phrase counts will be done in Microsoft Excel.  
        In addition to these planned techniques, the dataset used to build the system was analyzed by the researchers during development. The Bikol-Naga to English dictionary and sentence list were loaded into the database, counted, and checked for rows that were flagged for review and for Bikol terms that carry more than one English entry; the counts are reported in Chapter 4\.  

**Software Development Methodology**  
**![][image2]**  
Figure 3.2: Feature-Driven Development (FDD) Methodology \[12\]   
The researchers adopted Feature-Driven Development (FDD) \[12\] as the software development methodology for this project, as its feature-by-feature planning and delivery structure suits a small research team building a system whose core value lies in a welldefined set of discrete, independently testable translation and lookup features \[12\]. The phases of this methodology, as carried out for the system, are as follows:   
**Develop an Overall Model.** This phase establishes a high-level, shared understanding of the system's domain before any feature is built \[12\]. The team produced a high-level model of the system covering the translation engine, the corpus and dictionary data store, the user accounts, and the user-facing interface. The output of this phase is the overall model shown by the architecture design (Figure 3.4) and the data flow diagrams (Figures 3.5 to 3.8).    
**Build a Feature List.** . This phase breaks the overall model down into a list of small, client-valued features that can each be planned, designed, and built individually \[12\]. The team decomposed the system into six modules: user account and login, translation engine, mic (voice input), translation history, user administration, and the audit log. The result is the functional decomposition in Figure 4.1 and Table 4.1.   
**Plan by Feature.**  This phase sequences the features according to dependency, priority, and team ownership \[12\]. Core dictionary and corpus lookup was planned first, because every other translation feature depends on it; the grammar-based construction and the word-by-word fallback were planned after it, and the account, history, and administration features were planned around the translation engine.   
**Design by Feature.** This phase produces a short, feature-specific design before the implementation of that feature begins \[12\]. For each feature, the team prepared the database tables, the processing steps, and the screen that the feature needs; these designs are presented as the engine design, data models, and system models later in this chapter (Figures 3.9 to 3.16).   
           **Build by Feature.** This is the implementation phase, where each designed feature is coded, tested, and integrated into the overall system \[12\]. Each feature was implemented and integrated incrementally, and an automated test suite was extended with each feature. The result is the working system described in this chapter and tested as reported in Chapter 4\. 

**Requirement Analysis & Specifications**  
***Process Flow Models***  
The process flow of each module of the system is illustrated using Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 2.0, the graphical process-modeling standard maintained by the Object Management Group \[13\]. Figures 3.3a to 3.3f show the process flow of the six modules: user account and login, translation engine, mic (voice input), translation history, user administration, and audit log. In each figure, the lanes show who performs a step: the person using the module (the user or the administrator), the system, and, for the mic module, the browser of the device. The circle at the top is the start and the thick circle is the end. A rounded rectangle is a task: the person icon marks a step done by the person, the gear icon a step done by the system, and the envelope icon a message shown to the person. A diamond with an X is a decision in which only one path is taken.   
*![][image3]*  
        *Figure 3.3a: Process Flow of the User Account and Login Module (BPMN 2.0)*   
Figure 3.3a shows the process flow of the User Account and Login Module. The user enters the username and password and presses Sign in, and the system finds the account. If the account is missing, inactive, or locked, the system still checks a dummy password so that the response takes the same time, writes login\_failed to the activity log, and shows the same message that is used for every failed sign-in. Otherwise, the system checks the password. If the password is wrong, the system adds 1 to the failed attempts; at the fifth failed attempt it locks the account for 15 minutes and writes account\_locked, and before that it writes login\_failed. In both cases the same message is shown. If the password is correct, the system resets the failed attempts, records the last sign-in, starts the session, which lasts 8 hours, and writes login\_success. When the account carries a temporary password, the user must enter the current password and a new one; the system checks both, stores the new password in hashed form, and writes password\_changed. All of these paths lead to the same end. 

 *![][image4]*  
           *Figure 3.3b: Process Flow of the Translation Engine Module (BPMN 2.0)*   
Figure 3.3b shows the process flow of the Translation Engine Module. The user types Bikol-Naga text, or dictates it with the mic, and presses Translate. The system first checks the text; if it is empty or longer than 200 characters, it shows the matching message and the process ends. Otherwise, the engine tries four ways in order: (1) an exact match with a stored sentence or dictionary word; (2) the adaptation of a close stored sentence in which two words or fewer differ, with the changed words marked; (3) the construction of the sentence by the grammar module, only when the module understands every word, with the rules shown; and (4) when none of these applies, the text is split into sentences, each sentence goes through the same steps or is translated word by word, and the unknown words are marked. If no word can be translated, the system shows that no translation was found and suggests the closest stored sentence, if there is one. Otherwise, the result is labeled exact, adapted, grammar-built, rough (all words found), or partial (some words found), and the system adds 1 to the use count of each dictionary word found. The translation is saved to the history of the user only when the result is complete or partial, and it is saved before the result is returned. The system then shows the English text with its label and notes, and the user reads it. 

![][image5]  
              *Figure 3.3c: Process Flow of the Mic (Voice Input) Module (BPMN 2.0)*   
Figure 3.3c shows the process flow of the Mic (Voice Input) Module. It has three lanes because the speech is converted to text by the browser of the device and not by the system. The user presses the Mic button on the translator page. If the browser does not support speech recognition, the page shows that microphone access was denied or is not supported and that the user can type instead. Otherwise, the browser asks permission to use the microphone, and if permission is not given, the same message is shown. When permission is given, the user speaks a word, phrase, or sentence, and the browser turns the speech into text using the speech-to-text of the device, set to Filipino (fil-PH). If no speech is heard, the page shows that no speech was detected and asks the user to try again. Otherwise, the page adds the recognized text to the input box, up to 200 characters, and runs the translation as described for the Translation Engine Module (Figure 3.3b). The user then reads the English translation. 

![][image6]  
            *Figure 3.3d: Process Flow of the Translation History Module (BPMN 2.0)*   
Figure 3.3d shows the process flow of the Translation History Module. The user opens History, and the system shows the Active tab, which lists only the translations of that user, newest first, up to 500\. The user may archive one entry, which sets the archive time of that entry; archive all entries, which, after the user confirms, sets the archive time of all the active entries of the user; or, on the Archived tab, restore one entry, which clears its archive time. These actions apply only to the records of the user, and no entry is ever deleted. The system then updates the list on the screen, and the user sees the updated list. The saving of a translation to the history is part of the Translation Engine Module (Figure 3.3b). 

![][image7]  
            *Figure 3.3e: Process Flow of the User Administration Module (BPMN 2.0)*   
Figure 3.3e shows the process flow of the User Administration Module, which is available to the Administrator only. The Administrator opens User Administration, and the system lists the accounts, which can be searched by username and filtered by role and status. The Administrator then chooses one of five actions. To create an account, the username must have 3 to 30 characters (letters, numbers, dot, dash, or underscore) and must not be taken yet; the system creates the account with a one-time temporary password, stores only its hash, writes user\_created, and shows the temporary password once. To change a role, the system changes the role and writes role\_changed. To reset a password, the system issues a new temporary password, ends the old sessions of the account, writes password\_reset, and shows the new temporary password once. To deactivate an account, the system makes it unable to sign in and writes user\_deactivated. To reactivate an account, the system clears its failed attempts and lock and writes user\_reactivated. The system refuses to change the role of or deactivate the account of the Administrator who is signed in and the last active Administrator, and it refuses to reset the password of the Administrator who is signed in. 

![][image8]  
                   *Figure 3.3f: Process Flow of the Audit Log Module (BPMN 2.0)*   
Figure 3.3f shows the process flow of the Audit Log Module, which is shown on the screen as the activity log. The Administrator opens the Audit Log, and the system checks that the user is an Administrator; if not, it shows that the user does not have access to the page. Otherwise, the system reads the latest 200 entries, newest first, and shows the time, the person who did the action, the event, the account concerned, and the detail of each entry, which the Administrator reviews. The entries are written by the system by itself when someone signs in or fails to, is locked out, signs out, or changes a password, and when an Administrator creates, changes, deactivates, reactivates, or resets the password of an account. Passwords are never recorded. 

***Functional Requirements***  
*The functional requirements are grouped by module.* 

**1\. User Account and Login Module**   
1.1. The system shall require users to log in with an account before accessing any feature other than the login page.   
1.2. The system shall support three roles: Student and Teacher/Facilitator, which have the same access to the translation and translation history features, and Administrator, which has access to user management and the audit log only. The role shall be recorded in the user account.   
1.3. The system shall show the same generic message for every failed login, whether the username does not exist, the account is inactive or locked, or the password is wrong. 1.4. The system shall lock an account for 15 minutes after 5 consecutive failed login attempts.   
1.5. The system shall require a user who signs in with a temporary password to choose a new password before using any other feature.   
1.6. The system shall check a new password for length (at least 8 characters in this version, at most 128 characters) and reject passwords that are on a list of common passwords or that contain the username, without requiring particular character types. 1.7. The system shall keep the user signed in with a session cookie that cannot be read by page scripts and that expires after 8 hours, and shall end the sessions of an account whose password is changed or reset or which is deactivated. 

**2\. Translation Engine Module**   
2.1. The system shall accept Bikol-Naga text input (word, phrase, or sentence) typed by the user.   
2.2. The system shall process the input in this order: (a) a whole-input match with a sentence or word in the compiled dataset; (b) adaptation of a similar stored sentence that differs by at most two words found in the dictionary; (c) construction of the sentence with the grammar rules when every word is understood; and (d) a word-by-word translation.   
2.3. The system shall display the translated English output to the user within 3 seconds for typed input of up to 200 characters, under a normal load of up to 10 users using the system at the same time.    
2.4. The system shall accept typed input of up to 200 characters (about one sentence); when the input is longer, the system shall ask the user to shorten it, and when the input is empty, the system shall ask the user to enter text.   
2.5. When only some of the words in the input are found, the system shall display the translation of the recognized words, keep the unrecognized words in their original Bikol-Naga form, and mark them so that the user can see which words were not translated.   
2.6. When none of the words in the input are found, the system shall display a "no translation found" message and advise the user to check the spelling or try a simpler word or phrase.   
2.7. When a translation cannot be completed because of a system error, the system shall display a message that the translation failed and allow the user to try again.   
2.8. The system shall label every result with how it was produced (exact, adapted, grammar-built, or word-by-word), shall mark the changed words and name the source sentence of an adapted result, and shall list the grammar rules and sources used for a grammar-built result.   
2.9. The system shall never guess the meaning of a word that is not in the dictionary; it shall keep the word as written, and, where possible, suggest the closest stored sentence or a spelling.   
**3\. Mic (Voice Input) Module**   
3.1. The system shall provide a microphone (mic) button that lets the user dictate BikolNaga input by voice.   
3.2. The system shall use the browser's built-in speech-to-text capability to convert the dictated speech into text before passing it to the Translation Engine Module. 

**4\. Translation History Module**   
4.1. The system shall maintain a record of each logged-in user's past translations that produced a result.   
4.2. The system shall allow the user to view their own translation history at any time after logging in, and shall not show any user's history to another user or to the Administrator. 4.3. The system shall allow the user to archive and restore history entries and to archive all entries, and shall never delete a history entry.   
**5\. User Administration Module**   
5.1. The system shall allow the Administrator to create an account with a username and a role; the system shall generate a one-time temporary password that is shown once and is stored only as a hash.   
5.2. The system shall allow the Administrator to change the role of another user and to reset the password of another user, which shall again be a temporary password.   
5.3. The system shall allow the Administrator to deactivate and reactivate accounts; an inactive account cannot log in and its history is kept.   
5.4. The system shall not allow the Administrator to change their own role, deactivate their own account, or leave the system with no active Administrator.   
5.5. The system shall allow the Administrator to list users and to search them by username, role, and status. 

**6\. Audit Log Module**   
6.1. The system shall record successful and failed logins, account lockouts, password changes and resets, and account creation, role change, deactivation, and reactivation, each with the time, the acting user, the affected user, and a detail.   
6.2. The system shall allow the Administrator to view the most recent 200 audit log entries.

***Non-functional Requirements***  
*List of specific and detailed qualities or characteristics that a system must possess to be considered successful, but do not directly relate to the specific tasks or functions it performs*  
**1\. Performance.**   
a. The system must return a translation result within 3 seconds for typed input of up to 200 characters, under a normal load of up to 10 users using the system at the same time.   
**2\. Security.**   
a. The system must restrict access to a user's translation history to that authenticated user's own account only.   
b. Passwords must be stored only as salted hashes.   
c. A request that changes data must carry a header that a page from another site cannot add (protection against cross-site request forgery).   
d. Securityrelevant events must be written to the audit log.   
**3\. Reliability.**   
a. The system must maintain a consistently available service throughout the pilot deployment period, with minimal unplanned downtime.   
**4\. Usability**.   
a. The system's interface must be understandable and operable by UNC students, faculty, and facilitators with no prior technical training, given the system's intended walk-up, in-the-moment use case.   
**5\. Maintainability**.   
a. The system's dictionary and corpus must be structured so that the development team can extend or correct entries without requiring changes to the underlying translation code.   
b. The data must be loaded from plain data files, and loading must be safe to repeat without deleting accounts or history. 

***Use Cases***  
***Role Separation.** In this version of the system, the Student and Teacher/Facilitator roles have the same access: both can log in, translate text by typing or by voice, and view and archive their own translation history, and no feature is limited to one role. The two roles are still kept as separate account types for two reasons. First, the study involves two 47 kinds of users, students who use the tool for their own translation needs and teachers and facilitators who recommend or demonstrate it to students, and the researchers need to tell which group a user belongs to so that the feedback collected during the pilot and user acceptance testing can be reported separately for each group. Second, because the role is stored in each user account, role-specific features can be added in future work without redesigning the accounts; such features are outside the scope of this study. The Administrator role is different in kind: it can manage accounts and read the audit log, and it cannot translate or see any user's history.*   
**1\. Scenario: Log In to the System**   
a. Actor(s): Student, Teacher/Facilitator, or Administrator   
b. Precondition: The user has an active account created by the Administrator.   
c. Postcondition: The user is signed in and sees the pages that belong to the role; a user with a temporary password must first choose a new one.   
d. Steps:   
    i. The user opens the system in a web browser.   
    ii. The user enters the username and password.   
   iii. The system verifies the credentials; for any failure it shows the same message and, after five failures, locks the account for 15 minutes.   
   iv. The system signs the user in and records the event in the audit log.   
   v. If the password is temporary, the system asks the user to choose a new password before anything else. 

**2\. Scenario: Translate a Bikol-Naga Phrase by Typing**   
a. Actor(s): Student or Teacher/Facilitator   
b. Precondition: The user is logged in to the system.   
c. Postcondition: The user receives the English translation, labeled with how it was produced, and it is saved to the translation history unless nothing was found.   
d. Steps:   
     i. The user types a Bikol-Naga word, phrase, or sentence into the input field (up to 200 characters).  
       ii. The user submits the input for translation.   
    iii. The system processes the input through the Translation Engine Module (exact match, adapted example, grammar rules, word-by-word).   
    iv. The system saves the result to the user's translation history and displays the English translation with its label, its notes, and any marked words. 

**3\. Scenario: Translate a Bikol-Naga Phrase by Voice Dictation**   
a. Actor(s): Student or Teacher/Facilitator   
b. Precondition: The user is logged in and has granted microphone access.   
c. Postcondition: The user receives the English translation of the dictated input, which is saved to the translation history.   
d. Steps:   
        i. The user presses the mic button.   
        ii. The user speaks a Bikol-Naga word, phrase, or sentence.   
   iii. The Mic Module converts the spoken input into text using the browser's speechto-text capability.   
    iv. The system passes the resulting text to the Translation Engine Module and displays the translation as in the typing scenario. 

**4\. Scenario: View and Archive Translation History**   
a. Actor(s): Student or Teacher/Facilitator   
b. Precondition: The user is logged in and has at least one past translation on record.   
c. Postcondition: The user views their own past translations and may archive or restore them; no entry is deleted.   
d. Steps:    
      i. The user opens the translation history section.   
     ii. The system retrieves only the records of the logged-in user's account.   
    iii. The system displays the list; the user may archive or restore an entry, or archive all entries. 

**5\. Scenario: Manage User Accounts**   
a. Actor(s): Administrator   
b. Precondition: The Administrator is logged in.   
c. Postcondition: The account change is applied, the affected user's sessions end, and the action is in the audit log.   
d. Steps:   
      i. The Administrator opens the user administration page and may search users by username, role, or status.   
     ii. The Administrator creates an account, changes a role, resets a password, or deactivates or reactivates an account.   
    iii. For a new account or a reset, the system generates a one-time temporary password, shows it once, and stores only its hash. iv. The system writes the action to the audit log. 

**6\. Scenario: View the Audit Log**   
a. Actor(s): Administrator   
b. Precondition: The Administrator is logged in.   
c. Postcondition: The Administrator sees the most recent audit log entries.   
d. Steps:   
         i. The Administrator opens the audit log page.   
         ii. The system lists the latest 200 entries with time, actor, action, target, and detail. 

**System Design**  
***System Architecture***  
*Illustration of the overall structure and organization of the system, including its components, their relationships, and how they interact.*   
![][image9]  
Figure 3.4: Architecture Design of the Proposed System  

The system follows a three-tier architecture consisting of a client tier, an application tier, and a data tier. The client tier is a browser-based React interface, accessible from desktop or mobile web browsers, through which users log in, submit Bikol-Naga text (typed or dictated with the browser's speech-to-text), view the English translation, and manage their translation history, and through which the Administrator manages accounts and reads the audit log. The application tier is a Flask application. Its routes check the session, the role, and the request header on every call, and pass the work to the authentication and user administration functions, to the translation engine, or to the audit logger. The translation engine loads the dictionary and the corpus from the database (and reloads them only when the data has changed), looks the input up in memory, and, when needed, calls the grammar module, which builds an English sentence from Bikol-Naga words and returns the rules and sources it used. The data tier is a SQLite database that stores the user accounts, the dictionary, the corpus, each user's history, and the audit log; it is filled from the researchers' dataset files by an initialization script, which can be run again without deleting accounts or history. This separation allows the translation engine and the data to be updated independently of the user interface, supporting the maintainability requirement identified above. 

***Data Flow Models***  
*Illustrations of the flow of data through the system, showing the input, processing, and output stages.*   
![][image10]  
Figure 3.5: Context Diagram of the Proposed System (Gane-Sarson Notation) 

The context diagram positions the system, labeled as Process 0 (UNC Translator), between three external entities: Student, Teacher/Facilitator, and Administrator. The Student and the Teacher/Facilitator send login credentials, a new password, Bikol-Naga text or voice input, and history requests (view, archive, restore), and receive the login result and messages, the English translation with its notes, and the history records. The Administrator sends login credentials, user account actions, and activity log requests, and  receives the user list, one-time temporary passwords, and activity log records. The EIE Program coordinators who take part in this study are interviewed as key informants and are not users of the system, and updates to the dictionary and corpus are made by the development team, so they are not external entities in the diagrams. 

*![][image11]*  
Figure 3.6: Level 0 Data Flow Diagram of the Proposed System (Gane-Sarson Notation) 

        The Level 0 diagram decomposes the system into four processes. Process 1 (Log In and Change Password) verifies credentials against the User Accounts data store (D1) and lets a user choose a new password. Process 2 (Translate Text) accepts typed or micdictated Bikol-Naga input, looks it up in the Dictionary and Corpus data store (D2), returns the English translation and notes, and saves a translation record to the Translation History data store (D3).
