Process 3 (Manage Translation History) retrieves, archives, and restores a user's own records in D3. Process 4 (Manage User Accounts) lets the Administrator change the accounts in D1 and read and write the Activity Log data store (D4). 

*![][image12]*  
               Figure 3.7: Level 1 Data Flow Diagram — Process 2, Translate Text   
                
               The Level 1 diagram for Process 2 decomposes translation into seven subprocesses: 2.1 (Accept Typed or Spoken Input), 2.2 (Convert Speech to Text, the Mic Module, used only for voice input), 2.3 (Validate, Normalize and Split Input), 2.4 (Look Up Dictionary and Corpus, which returns an exact or adapted translation or passes the input on), 2.5 (Build Sentence with Grammar Rules), 2.6 (Compose Result and Messages), and 2.7 (Save to Translation History). A data flow diagram does not show the timing of steps; the order, in which the translation is saved to the history before it is displayed, is shown in the Activity and Sequence diagrams (Figures 3.14 and 3.15). 

![][image13]  
            Figure 3.8: Level 1 Data Flow Diagram \- Process 4, Manage User Accounts (GaneSarson Notation)   
          The Level 1 diagram for Process 4 decomposes user administration into five subprocesses: 4.1 (Create User Account), 4.2 (Change Role), 4.3 (Reset Password), 4.4 (Deactivate or Reactivate Account), and 4.5 (List, Search and Filter Users; View Activity Log). All five sub-processes use the User Accounts data store (D1) and the Activity Log data store (D4) through the bus on the right of the figure: the first four write account records and action records, and the fifth reads them. Creating an account and resetting a password return a one-time temporary password to the Administrator.   
Translation Design Engine  
![][image14]  
                 Figure 3.9: Lookup Order of the Translation Engine   
            Figure 3.9 shows what the translation engine does with an input. After the length check and the normalization of the text, the engine looks at the whole input first. A whole input match in the dataset is shown as the researchers' own English. Otherwise, an input that differs from a stored sentence by one or two words that are in the dictionary is adapted: the stored English is reused, the changed words are replaced and marked, and the source sentence is shown. Otherwise, the grammar module tries to build the sentence from rules, which succeeds only if every word is understood. If it does not, the input is split into sentences and translated word by word, with grammar words left out, unknown words kept as written and marked, and the closest stored sentence suggested. If no word at all is recognized, the system shows the "no translation found" message. Results that are not empty are saved to the history and add 1 to the use count of the words found.   
![][image15]  
                                    Figure 3.10: Flow of the Grammar Module   
                   Figure 3.10 shows the flow inside the grammar module. The module first joins verb prefixes that were typed apart from their root (for example, ma kakan is read as makakan) and re-orders sentences in the Tagalog subject-first pattern with ay, which Mintz does not list as a Bikol-Naga word \[14\]. It then decides whether the sentence is a question (with a question word such as ano, sain, nuarin, siisay, pano, ta'no, or gurano) or one of the supported sentence types: verbal, desire (gusto), existential (may, igwa, mayo'), equational, or a subject-less phrase. The noun-phrase rules handle the markers an, si, nin, kan, ni, and sa, the plural mga, the possessive pronouns placed after a noun, and place names that are not in the dictionary, which are kept as written after sa. The verb rules read the tense and focus from the prefix and build the English form. If no pattern fits or a word is not understood, the module reports that it cannot parse the sentence and the engine falls back to the word-by-word result. Every built sentence carries notes that cite the source of each rule. 

***Data Dictionary***  
Tables 3.1 to 3.6 describe the data items kept in the data stores shown in the Level 0 diagram (Figure 3.6): D1 User Accounts (Table 3.1), D2 Dictionary and Corpus (Tables 3.2 to 3.4), D3 Translation History (Table 3.5), and D4 Activity Log (Table 3.6). The core data items used by the translation engine are the Bikol-Naga source term, its English target term or phrase, an example sentence pair, and a frequency-of-use indicator that increases each time a word is found in a translation. The field names and data types are those of the implemented database. 

                         Table 3.1: Data Dictionary for User Accounts (D1) 

| Field | Data type | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| user\_id (PK) | INTEGER | Unique number of the account, assigned automatically. |
| username | TEXT, unique | Login name, 3 to 30 letters, numbers, dot, dash, or underscore; not case-sensitive. |
| password | TEXT | Scrypt hash of the password with its salt; the password itself is never stored. |
| role | TEXT | Student, Teacher/Facilitator, or Administrator. |
| is\_active | INTEGER | 1 if the account may log in, 0 if it has been deactivated. |
| must\_change\_password | INTEGER | 1 while the password is a temporary one chosen by the system. |
| failed\_attempts | INTEGER | Number of consecutive failed logins; set back to 0 on success or lockout. |
| locked\_until | TEXT, null | Time until which the account is locked; empty if not locked. |
| created\_at | TEXT | Date and time the account was created (UTC). |
| last\_login\_at | TEXT, null | Date and time of the last successful login (UTC). |

| Field | Data type | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| term\_id (PK) | INTEGER | Unique number of the Bikol-Naga term. |
| bikol\_term | TEXT, unique | The Bikol-Naga word or fixed expression; not case-sensitive. |
| frequency\_of\_use | INTEGER | Number of translations in which the term was found. |

| :---- | :---- | :---- |

| Field | Data type | Description |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

***Data Models***   
*Illustrations of the database, including tables, fields, data types, and relationships*  
*![][image16]*  
Figure 3.11: Entity-Relationship Data Model of the Proposed System (Crow's Foot Notation)   
Figure 3.11 shows the conceptual entity-relationship model, which has six entities. User holds each account's login credentials, role, and status. Term holds individual BikolNaga dictionary entries, and each Term has one or more Translation records holding its English equivalent. CorpusSentence holds parallel Bikol-Naga and English sentence pairs, and AuditLog holds the security events; both stand alone, with no link to the other entities. History records each translation a user makes. A User makes many History records, and a Term has many Translations. A History record refers to a Translation only when a stored translation matched the whole input, so that link is optional.  

![][image17]  
Figure 3.12: Relational Data Model of the Proposed System (Crow's Foot Notation)   
Figure 3.12 shows the same model as relational tables, with primary keys (PK), foreign keys (FK), and the data types used in the Data Dictionary (Tables 3.1 to 3.6). HISTORY.user\_id refers to USER, HISTORY.translation\_id refers to TRANSLATION and may be left blank when no stored translation matched the whole input, and TRANSLATION.term\_id refers to TERM. CORPUS\_SENTENCE and AUDIT\_LOG have no foreign keys; the audit log keeps the username as text so that the record remains readable if an account is later changed.

*Set of diagrams that model the different aspects of a system such as its structure and behavior*  
![][image18]  
Figure 3.13: Use Case Diagram of the Proposed System (UML)   
Figure 3.13 shows who uses the system and what they can do. Student and Teacher/Facilitator have identical access, so they are drawn as one actor, and each can log in and out, change the password, translate text, view the translation history, and archive and restore history entries; translating can be extended by using the mic input and by reading how a sentence was built. The Administrator can log in and out, change the password, manage user accounts, and view the audit log, and cannot translate.    
![][image19]  
Figure 3.14: Activity Diagram of the Proposed System (UML)    
Figure 3.14 traces the activities of the three roles. After the user logs in, the system shows a generic error and asks again if the login fails, and asks for a new password if the password is temporary. A student or teacher goes to the translator page, enters or speaks the text, presses Translate, and reads the result and its status label; the user may then open the history to view, archive, or restore entries, translate again, or log out. The Administrator goes to the admin page and either manages users (create, change role, reset password, deactivate or reactivate, search) or views the audit log, and may continue or log out. 

![][image20]  
Figure 3.15: Sequence Diagram of the Translation Process (UML)   
Figure 3.15 shows the order of messages between the user, the React interface, the Flask API, the translation engine, the grammar module, and the SQLite database. The user types or speaks the text and the interface sends it to the API with the session cookie and the request header. The API checks the session, the role, and the header, then passes the text to the engine. The engine rejects empty input and input of more than 200 characters, loads the dictionary and the corpus from the database (it reloads them only when the data has changed), and looks up the whole input in memory. If there is an exact or adapted match, the stored result is used; otherwise the engine asks the grammar module to build the sentence, and, if the module cannot, falls back to the word-by-word result. The engine adds 1 to the use count of each word found and returns the result to the API. The API saves the translation to the user's history only when the result is complete or partial, and returns the result to the interface, which shows the English text, the status label, and the notes.  

![][image21]  
Figure 3.16: Class Diagram of the Proposed System (UML)   
Figure 3.16 shows the main classes of the system. User holds the account data and the login operations. The Student / TeacherFacilitator class, which stands for the two roles that have the same access, and the Administrator class specialize it; the first uses the TranslationEngine and keeps its own history, and the Administrator manages accounts and views the audit log, which the system fills with login and account events. Term, Translation, CorpusSentence, HistoryEntry, and AuditLog correspond to the entities in the data model, with the same attributes and relationships. TranslationEngine receives a translation request, reads Term, Translation, and CorpusSentence data, and uses Grammar to build the sentence. It keeps only an in-memory copy of the dictionary and the corpus that it loads from the database, so it does not appear in the data model. 

**Testing and Evaluation**  
Testing and evaluation serve two different purposes in this study. Software testing checks whether the system works as specified in the functional and non-functional requirements; each test case ends in a pass or a fail. Research evaluation checks how good the translations are and how usable the system is for its intended users, using human validators and UAT participants; it ends in ratings and percentages that are reported, not passed or failed. This proposal describes the planned procedures only. The test inputs, actual results, and ratings will be recorded and reported in the final manuscript. Testing Methods below describe the software testing and how the UAT is carried out, and Evaluation Criteria describe how the results of the research evaluation are scored. 

***Testing Methods***

Testing and evaluation serve two different purposes in this study. Software testing checks whether the system works as specified in the functional and non-functional requirements; each test case ends in a pass or a fail. Research evaluation checks how good the translations are and how usable the system is for its intended users, using human validators and UAT participants; it ends in ratings and percentages that are reported, not passed or failed. The software tests were carried out by the researchers during development; the human validation and the UAT are planned procedures that had not been carried out when this manuscript was prepared. Testing Methods below describe the software testing and how the UAT is carried out, and Evaluation Criteria describe how the results of the research evaluation are scored. 

**Unit Testing:** Individual components were tested independently against known Bikol-Naga input and expected output: the password rules, the lockout counter, the input length check, the dictionary and corpus lookup, the adaptation of a stored sentence, and each grammar rule.   
**Integration Testing:** The components were tested together through the web routes, using a test client and a temporary database loaded with the researchers' dataset, to verify that input flows correctly from the request to the final English translation and the saved history record, and that the role checks work on every route.   
**System Testing:** The complete system was tested against the functional requirements, including response time, correct handling of unrecognized input, history privacy, and user administration. The test set that compares the output with the researchers' English is described in Chapter 4\. Testing against a set of sentences verified by a Bikol speaker has not been done yet HINDI PA PO KASE NAMIN NA KUMPLETO SI SURVEY.  
**Error Handling Testing:** The test cases include empty input, input longer than 200 characters, input with some unrecognized words, input with no recognized words, and unauthorized requests, to confirm that each one shows the message specified in the functional requirements.  
**Test Cases and Pass Criteria:** Table 3.7 lists the test cases, which are based on the functional and non-functional requirements, the kind of input used for each, and the expected result that serves as its pass criterion. A test case passes when the observed result matches the expected result. The automated test suite contains 42 tests; they were all run and all passed.

           **User Acceptance Testing (UAT):** A sample of UNC students, faculty, and EIE Program facilitators will use the system with real, spontaneous Bikol-Naga input during a pilot period, following guided scenarios based on the use case scenarios in this chapter (log in, translate by typing, translate by voice dictation, and view translation history), and will then answer a post-use questionnaire on ease of learning, ease of use, and satisfaction with the translation results. The researchers will record whether each participant completed each scenario, and will use the feedback to refine the corpus and interface prior to final evaluation. The number of participants in each group, the final questionnaire items, and the rating scale will be confirmed with the adviser before the pilot. 

***Evaluation Criteria***  
	**Technique Selection:** The NLP technique and translation approach were selected during the development phase using four criteria. (1) Fit with the corpus: the technique must be workable with the size and coverage of the Bikol-Naga to English corpus and dictionary the researchers were able to compile, since large parallel corpora are generally unavailable for low-resource language pairs \[9\]. (2) Translation accuracy: each candidate technique is run on the same set of sentence pairs, and its output is compared with the researchers' English; human validators are to rate the share of outputs that are correct or acceptable. (3) Response time: the response time per translation request must meet the target set in the non-functional requirements (3 seconds for typed input of up to 200 characters). (4) Feasibility: the technique must be implementable and maintainable by the researchers with Python-based libraries within the project timeline. The comparison, the reason for the choice, and the configuration of the selected technique are documented in Chapter 4\. No numeric pass mark is set for translation accuracy.   
       **Translation Quality:** Translation quality is evaluated on a held-out set of BikolNaga to English sentence pairs, which serves as the reference translations. Two kinds of measurement are used. The first is an automated, developer-side measurement: the word-overlap F1 between the system's English and the researchers' English for the same sentence, where the sentence itself is left out of the data that the system can use; this is not a BLEU score and not a judgment of quality. The second is a human rating: validators who are fluent in both Bikol-Naga and English compare each system output with its reference and rate it as correct, acceptable, or incorrect. The definition of each rating will be set with the adviser before the evaluation. Accuracy is the number of outputs rated correct or acceptable divided by the total number of outputs rated, multiplied by 100, and the count for each rating is reported as well. The number of validators, the size of the test set, and how disagreements between validators are settled will be set with the adviser. No numeric pass mark is set for translation accuracy; the percentage is reported as the result and interpreted in light of the size of the corpus and the test set.   
        **Functionality:** Evaluated by confirming that all functional requirements listed in this chapter, including text input, voice input, translation output, translation history, user administration, and the audit log, operate as specified. Indicators: percentage of specified features successfully implemented; percentage of test cases passed during system testing; number of defects found during UAT. 

        **Reliability:** Evaluated through the researchers' record of system failures and errors observed during the pilot deployment period. Indicators: number of system failures recorded during the pilot; percentage of translation requests completed without a system error; consistency of output for repeated identical input.   
    **Performance:** Evaluated through the response time per translation request, measured as described under Response Time Testing, and through translation accuracy, measured as described under Translation Quality. Indicators: average and maximum response time per request; number of requests that took longer than 3 seconds; performance under concurrent multi-user access; percentage of system translations rated correct or acceptable by human validators against the reference set.   
       **Usability:** Evaluated through a post-use questionnaire given to UAT participants and through task completion during the guided UAT scenarios. Indicators: the average rating for each questionnaire item and overall (Table 3.8), reported separately for students and for teachers and facilitators, following the two user roles; the task completion rate (tasks completed divided by tasks assigned, multiplied by 100); and qualitative feedback on interface clarity. Acceptability, as stated in the objectives of the study, is assessed through the same post-use questionnaire, in particular the item on how useful the translations received were. 

                      **Table 3.8: Planned Post-Use Questionnaire Items**

| No. | Item (rated 1 to 5\) |
| :---- | :---- |
| 1 | I can enter Bikol-Naga text, by typing or by voice, and get a translation without help. |
| 2 | I can open and read my translation history with little effort. |
| 3 | I can understand the system's messages and interface controls. |
| 4 | The system was easy to learn. |
| 5 | The English translations I received were useful for what I needed to say. |

          **Usability Scoring:** The questionnaire in Table 3.8 uses a proposed five-point Likert scale: 5 \= Strongly Agree, 4 \= Agree, 3 \= Neutral, 2 \= Disagree, and 1 \= Strongly Disagree. The mean of an item is the sum of the ratings given to that item divided by the number of valid responses to it, and the overall usability mean is the average of the item means. The ranges used to interpret the means will be set with the adviser together with the questionnaire. An item left blank is not counted: it is left out of that item's mean, the number of valid responses for each item is reported, and a questionnaire with no answered items is excluded. The items are the planned questionnaire and may be refined with the adviser before the pilot.   
            **Security:** Evaluated by verifying that a user's translation history is accessible only to that authenticated user and that the account protections work as specified. Users must log in with an account before using the system, and passwords are stored only as scrypt hashes with a random salt (Table 3.1) \[21\]. Each translation history request returns only the records that belong to the logged-in user's account. Every request that changes data must carry the X-Requested-With header, the session cookie cannot be read by page scripts and is limited to the same site, the login shows one generic message for every failure, an account is locked for 15 minutes after 5 failed attempts, a temporary password must be changed at first sign-in, and security events are written to the audit log, following the guidance in \[22\], \[23\], and \[24\]. Verified by: (1) checking that passwords are not stored as plain text; (2) access-control test cases, in which one logged-in user tries to open another user's translation history, a visitor who has not logged in tries to open the translation and history pages, and a student tries to use the administrator pages. Indicators: result of each access-control test case (refused or allowed); number of unauthorized access attempts successfully blocked during testing; whether all stored passwords are hashed. The known weaknesses are listed under the Limitations of the Study. 

**CHAPTER 4**  
**DISCUSSION OF FINDINGS**  
This chapter presents the findings of the study according to the three specific problems stated in Chapter 1: the functional features and modules of the system, the Natural Language Processing technique and translation approach selected for it, and its performance in terms of translation accuracy, usability, and acceptability among its intended users. The findings on the features and modules come from the requirement analysis and specifications in Chapter 3\. The findings on the selected technique and on software testing come from the developed system and from measurements made by the researchers on their own dataset. The human validation of translations, the survey, and the user acceptance testing had not been carried out when this manuscript was prepared; the tables in which their results will be reported are shown with empty cells, and no result is stated for them. 

**Functional Features and Modules of the System**   
**Specific problem 1:** What functional features and modules must the proposed system possess to provide timely and relevant Bikol-Naga to English translation support to students, faculty, and facilitators within the context of the EIE Program?   
          Table 4.1 presents the modules of the system and the features of each module, together with the functional requirement that specifies it in Chapter 3\. 

                          Table 4.1: Modules and Features of the UNC Translator

| Module | Features | Requirement |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| User Account and Login | Log in and log out; generic login error; 15-minute lockout after 5 failed attempts; forced change of a temporary password; password length and common-password check; 8-hour session that ends when the password changes or the account is deactivated | 1.1 to 1.7 |
| Translation Engine | Typed input up to 200 characters; whole-input match; adapted example; grammar-built sentence; word-by-word fallback with marked unknown words; spelling hint and closest-sentence suggestion; several sentences in one input; result label and notes; "no translation found" and error messages | 2.1 to 2.10 |
| Mic (Voice Input) | Mic button; browser speech-to-text | 3.1, 3.2 |
| Translation History | Own history only; archive, restore, and archive all; no deletion | 4.1 to 4.3 |
| User Administration (Administrator) | Create account with one-time temporary password; change role; reset password; deactivate and reactivate; search and filter users; protection of the last administrator | 5.1 to 5.5 |
| Audit Log (Administrator) | Record of logins, lockouts, password changes and resets, and account changes; view of the latest 200 entries | 6.1, 6.2 |

![][image22]  
                    Figure 4.1: Functional Decomposition of the UNC Translator   
       In answer to the first specific problem, the system must possess six modules, User Account and Login, Translation Engine, Mic (Voice Input), Translation History, User Administration, and Audit Log, with the features listed in Table 4.1 and shown in Figure 4.1. The first four modules cover what Chapter 1 sets out for the system: logging in, translating Bikol-Naga input into English, optionally dictating the input by voice, and reviewing past translations. The last two were added during development because the system holds user accounts: accounts are created and managed by an Administrator, who has no access to what users translate, and the security events are recorded in an audit log, as the OWASP guidance recommends \[22, 24\]. Typed input and dictionary-based lookup also appear in the offline Tagalog-Bicol translation app of Velasco et al., which uses text-to-text input and a linear search algorithm for dictionary-based translation retrieval \[10\]. Voice input is kept as an optional feature that relies on the device's speechto-text, because automatic speech recognition for Bikol has been studied as a separate research effort \[8\], and most of the Philippine machine translation projects surveyed by Oco and Roxas focused only on text \[1\].   
To be completed po after data gathering since hindi pa po talaga kami nakatapos sa surveys kase andami po namin binago and yung results of the interviews with EIE Program coordinators and faculty facilitators and of the student survey described in Chapter 3\. The survey and the interviews have not been done yet. 

**Natural Language Processing Technique and Translation Approach**   
**Specific problem 2:** Which Natural Language Processing technique and translation approach best meet the selection criteria (fit with the size and coverage of the compiled Bikol-Naga corpus, translation accuracy, response time, and feasibility of implementation) for translating common campus-related vocabulary from Bikol-Naga to English, given the limited size of existing digital Bikol-Naga language resources? 

        Table 4.2 lists the approaches used in the machine translation studies reviewed in Chapter 2\. 

         Table 4.2: Approaches Used in the Reviewed Machine Translation Studies 

| Study | Language pair | Approach | Evaluation reported |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Fernandez et al., as reported in \[1\] | Bikol-English (both directions) | Statistical | Not reported in the survey \[1\] |
| Sagum \[4\] | Bicolano-Tagalog (both directions) | Transfer-based with dictionaries, rules, and statistical methods | Scores of 74.75% and 71.7%; the metric and corpus are not stated in the abstract \[4\] |
| Velasco et al. \[10\] | Tagalog-Bicol | Rule-based with linear dictionary search | Human assessment by native speakers and usability testing |
| Adlaon and Marcos \[5\] | Cebuano-Filipino | Neural (language resource building) | Corpus construction method \[5\] |
| Ranathunga et al. \[9\] | Low-resource languages (survey) | Neural | Neural MT performs sub-optimally on low-resource pairs \[9\] |

           The Bikol-related studies in Table 4.2 used statistical \[1\], transfer-based \[4\], and rule-based \[10\] approaches, while neural machine translation, per the survey of Ranathunga et al., still performs sub-optimally on low-resource language pairs because large parallel corpora are unavailable \[9\]. This is why the technique for the system was selected during development, according to the size and coverage of the Bikol-Naga corpus the researchers were able to compile, and was not decided in advance.   
          
          Table 4.3 shows the data that is currently loaded into the system and that determines which technique can work. The dictionary and the corpus are still being completed, so these counts will change.    
                               Table 4.3: Data Loaded into the System 

| Item | Count |
| :---- | :---- |
| Dictionary terms | 2,049 |
| English translations of the terms (some terms have two or more) | 2,528 |
| Corpus phrases and sentences | 3,786 |
| Rows not loaded because they need review | 532 |
| Terms with more than one English entry (the first is the primary translation) | 357 |

           The dataset has about two thousand words and under four thousand sentence pairs. This is far too small to train a neural model \[9\], but it is enough for dictionary lookup, example-based adaptation, and a rule-based sentence builder, which need no training. Of the 532 rows that were not loaded, 305 gave a different English for the same Bikol text, 147 had a slash or variant in the Bikol side, 60 could not be split into the three columns, and 20 appeared to be cut off; these rows are listed for the researchers to correct and to load again.   
              Table 4.4 compares the candidate techniques on the four selection criteria. The accuracy figures are developer-side measurements. For the leave-one-out test, each of the 2,310 corpus sentences of four or more words was taken out of the data in turn and translated by the rest of the system, so that the sentence was unseen. For the grammar module alone, every one of the 3,786 sentences was given to the module without any other part of the engine. In both tests the output was compared with the researchers' English by word-overlap F1, a score between 0 and 1\. This is not a BLEU score and not a human judgment of quality.   
           Table 4.4: Comparison of Candidate Techniques on the Selection Criteria 

| Candidate technique | Fit with the corpus | Translation accuracy (developer-side) | Response time | Feasibility |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Neural machine translation | Poor: needs large parallel corpora \[9\] | Not implemented or tested | Not tested | Low: no large corpus; training cost |
| Whole-input lookup only | Fits | Output only for inputs that are stored; none for unseen sentences | Not measured separately | High |
| Word-by-word dictionary lookup only | Fits | Output labeled rough; not a correct sentence; 10.5% of unseen sentences end here and 60.7% end as partial output | Not measured separately | High |
| Example-based adaptation \[16\] | Fits | Adapted output for 19.0% of unseen sentences (438 of 2,310); mean F1 0.82 | Not measured separately | High |
| Grammar rules \[14, 15\] | Fits; needs the dictionary and verb categories | Built a sentence for 20.6% of all 3,786 sentences (781); mean F1 0.68; for 9.2% of unseen sentences that adaptation did not cover (212 of 2,310); mean F1 0.71 | Not measured separately | Medium: rules must be written and checked against the sources |
| Selected: all of the above in the order exact, adapted, grammar-built, word-by-word | Fits | A complete sentence (adapted or grammar-built) for 28.1% of unseen sentences (650 of 2,310); the other 71.9% receive only rough, partial, or no output | Whole engine: mean 5.5 to 7.4 ms for 1 user; 18.7 to 27.5 ms for 10 users | Medium |

*Response times are from the system's translate function in the researchers' test environment. Percentages are shares of the 2,310 sentences of four or more words, except where stated.* 

      The technique selected is therefore a lookup-first, rule-based hybrid, which combines the dictionary-driven design reported by Velasco et al. \[10\] with example-based adaptation \[16\] and with grammar rules taken from the published descriptions of Bikol \[14, 15\]. The order of the steps follows the measured quality: adapted output has the higher mean word overlap (0.82 against 0.71 for grammar-built output), so it is tried first, and the whole-input match comes before both because it is the researchers' own English. Each step is used only when the one before it does not apply, and each result carries a label so the user can see how much to trust it.   
      Three observations qualify these findings. First, the F1 score counts shared words and does not judge meaning; in the researchers' check of sample outputs, most of the difference between the grammar-built English and the dataset's English was in word choice and not in word order, but this check was informal. Second, the grammar module is deliberately cautious: it builds a sentence only when it understands every word, because a wrong sentence that looks correct is worse than a marked rough result, so 79.4% of the sentences in the dataset are not built by grammar alone. Third, questions beyond the supported question words, comparison, ability (maka-), and the \-on, \-an, and i- verb voices are not supported, and these fall back to the word-by-word result. The selected technique and these figures are to be confirmed against a set of sentences verified by a Bikol speaker. MAGHAHANAP PO KAMI NG MGA POSSIBLE NA MAKAKAHELP.  

**Performance of the Developed System in Terms of Translation Accuracy, Usability, and Acceptability**   
**Specific problem 3:** To what extent does the developed system perform in terms of translation accuracy and in terms of usability and acceptability among its intended UNC users?   
         **Software testing.** The automated test suite of 42 tests, summarized in Table 3.7, was run on the final version of the system and all 42 tests passed. They cover the password hashing, the generic login error, the lockout, the request header, the role checks, the input rules, the exact, adapted, grammar-built, and word-by-word results, the privacy and archiving of the history, and the user administration and audit log functions. Two test cases remain: voice input in a browser, and response time on the pilot server. A passing test shows that the system does what the researchers specified; it does not show that a translation is correct.   
           **Response time.** Table 4.5 reports the response time of the translate function in the researchers' test environment, with requests sent in the same program as the server. This measures the work of the engine and the database and not the network or a pilot server.

To be completed after the human validation and the user acceptance testing: the discussion of the results in Tables 4.6 and 4.7, answering the third specific problem and comparing the findings with the related studies. 

What the evidence supports at this time is limited to three points. The system performs its specified functions and meets the 3-second requirement in the test environment. Its translations are as reliable as the dataset behind them: an exact match is the researchers' own English, an adapted result is usually close to it (mean F1 0.82 on unseen sentences), a grammar-built result is a reasonable but unverified attempt (mean F1 0.71 on unseen sentences), and everything else is clearly labeled as rough. And for most unseen sentences (71.9% in the test) the system can offer only partial help, which is consistent with the limits of a small corpus noted in the literature \[1, 5, 9\].

**CURRICULUM VITAE**

The following annotations summarize each source cited in this study and explain its specific relevance to the present research. 

**\[1\] Nathaniel Oco and Rachel Edita Roxas. 2018\. A Survey of Machine Translation Work in the Philippines: From 1998 to 2018\.**   
This survey reviews twenty years of Philippine machine translation research across languages such as Tagalog, Cebuano, Ilocano, Hiligaynon, and Bikol. It reports that Ilocano is the subject of three cited MT projects while Bikol, Cebuano, Kankanaey, Maranao, and Hiligaynon are each the subject of only one, and notes that in all the transfer-based projects the corpus size was limited and the vocabulary stayed within the available resources, and that most of the works presented focused only on text. This source establishes the empirical basis for treating Bikol-Naga as an understudied language in MT research and directly supports the study's stated research gap. The survey also reports the Bikol-English statistical machine translator by Fernandez et al. (2018); the researchers did not access that paper directly, so it is cited in this manuscript only through this survey. 

**\[2\] University of Nueva Caceres. n.d. Senior High School.**   
This official university webpage describes the UNC Senior High School program and includes the tagline "technology enabled, english immersive, and industry milieu." It is used as evidence that English immersion is an institutional theme at UNC, though it is drawn from the Senior High School program specifically rather than a university-wide EIE Program description. 

**\[3\] Osias Kit T. Kilag, Francisca T. Uy, Yancy B. Dogomeo, Rey Dela Cruz Jr., Princess Joy A. Matis, Rose Anne Gier, and Estrella G. Doroy. 2024\. English Language Education in the Philippines: Policy Landscape and Future Directions.**   
This paper reviews English Language Education policy in the Philippines and identifies policy fragmentation, shortages of qualified English teachers, and literature-focused curricula as persistent factors behind declining English competency among Filipino learners. It is used only as background on the national-level factors reported behind English competency among Filipino learners; it does not address UNC students or the EIE Program specifically. 

**\[4\] Ria A. Sagum. 2025\. Automated Translation between Bicolano and Tagalog using Transfer-Based Model.**   
This paper proposes a transfer-based bi-directional machine translation system for Bicolano and Tagalog, using language resources such as dictionaries and rules together with statistical approaches, and reports evaluation scores of 74.75% for Tagalog to Bicolano and 71.7% for Bicolano to Tagalog. Only the abstract was accessed; it does not state the evaluation metric or the corpus used. This source is the closest related system in target language family and is used to show that dictionary- and rule-based approaches have been applied to Bikol, although it does not translate into English. 

**\[5\] Kristine Mae M. Adlaon and Nelson Marcos. 2019\. Building the Language Resource for a Cebuano-Filipino Neural Machine Translation System.**   
This paper documents the process of building a parallel corpus for Cebuano and Filipino from biblical texts and web sources, and applying subword unit translation for verbs. It offers a useful reference for the corpus-building phase of the present study, despite targeting a different Philippine language pair. 

**\[6\] Google Translate Help. 2024\. What's new in Google Translate: More than 100 new languages.**   
This Google Translate Help page lists the languages added in Google's 2024 expansion, and its list includes "Bikol" without specifying a variety; the page is dated June 27, 2024\. It is used only to support the statements that Bikol was added to Google Translate in June 2024 and that the listing does not name a Bikol variety. The researchers did not test how well Google Translate handles Bikol. 

**\[7\] Joseph Jessie S. Oñate and Tiffany Lyn O. Pandes. 2025\. Exploratory Analysis of Rinconada Bikol Language-Nabua Text Corpus.**   
This study built a dedicated text corpus for Rinconada Bikol, a Bikol variety from Nabua, and used it to train a sentiment analyzer on 500 sentences. It is used as an example of corpus work on a different Bikol variety, which is outside the scope of the present study, and as evidence that small, purpose-built Bikol corpora can be built. 

**\[8\] Edward Harold Liao, Kim Ganareal, Chirstian Clarence Paguia, Cesar Agreda, Manolito Octaviano, and Ramon Rodriguez. 2019\. Towards the Development of Automatic Speech Recognition for Bikol and Kapampangan.**   
This paper reports the development of continuous speech recognition for Bikol and Kapampangan; only its abstract and publication details were reviewed by the researchers. It is used to show that speech recognition for Bikol has been studied as a separate research effort, which is why the present study does not attempt to build a custom BikolNaga speech recognizer, relying instead on general-purpose, device-provided speech-totext for its optional voice input feature. 

**\[9\] Surangika Ranathunga, En-Shiun Annie Lee, Marjana Prifti Skenduli, Ravi Shekhar, Mehreen Alam, and Rishemjit Kaur. 2021\. Neural Machine Translation for Low-Resource Languages: A Survey.**   
This survey finds that neural machine translation performs sub-optimally on low-resource language pairs relative to high-resource ones, due to the unavailability of large parallel corpora. It is cited in the Technical Background to explain why the specific NLP technique for this study cannot simply default to a neural approach, and instead needs to be selected during the development phase based on the actual size and coverage of the Bikol-Naga corpus the researchers are able to compile. 

**\[10\] Marienel N. Velasco, Mark Roland A. Gaiten, Ronald John R. Villar, Liah Allyzandra B. Santos, Minera Laiza C. Acosta, Dustin Kyle M. Garcia, Dgenlord Philippe C. Leynes, and Resylyn Z. Cabrera. 2025\. Bridging Language Gaps: an Offline Mobile Translation App for Filipino Dialects.**   
This paper describes an offline Tagalog-Bicol mobile translation app built with a rule-based NLP approach, a linear search algorithm for dictionary-based retrieval, and Python, evaluated by combining NLP-based methods with human assessment by native speakers. It is the closest related system in technology choices and evaluation approach, and is consistent with the present study's use of a Python-based, dictionary-driven design and its inclusion of human assessment in evaluation. 

**\[11\] Japhet Mari S. Garganera, Darrel M. Ocampo, and Cleo D. Gueriba. 2024\. English Language Proficiency and Communicative Competence among Graduate Students in Bicol Region, Philippines.**   
This study measured the English proficiency and communicative competence of graduate students at a graduate school in the Bicol Region using a standardized English test and found that most of the 118 respondents were at an intermediate level of communicative competence. It is used only as local context from the same region as UNC; its respondents were graduate students at one institution, so it does not describe UNC students. 

**\[12\] Stephen R. Palmer and John M. Felsing. 2002\. A Practical Guide to FeatureDriven Development.**   
This book describes Feature-Driven Development (FDD) and its five phases: Develop an Overall Model, Build a Feature List, Plan by Feature, Design by Feature, and Build by Feature. It is the basis for the software development methodology adopted in Chapter 3 of this study. 

**\[13\] Object Management Group (OMG). 2011\. Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN), Version 2.0.**   
This is the official specification for BPMN 2.0, the graphical process-modeling standard maintained by the Object Management Group. It is the notation standard used for the process flow diagram presented in Chapter 3 of this study. 

**\[14\] Malcolm W. Mintz. 1971\. Bikol Dictionary.**   
The open-access edition of this dictionary contains an introduction, "Use of the Dictionary," that describes the affixes, tenses, plurals, markers, and pronouns of Bikol, and dictionary entries with example sentences. It is the main source of the grammar rules in the translation engine, and each grammar-built result names the entry it relies on. The researchers did not read Mintz's separate Bikol Grammar Notes, and it is not used. 

**\[15\] Jon Epstein. 1967\. Standard Bikol.**   
A Peace Corps language course text. The scanned copy is partly illegible, so only the legible parts, on equational sentences, markers, and negation, were used as a second source for the grammar rules. 

**\[16\] Makoto Nagao. 1984\. A Framework of a Mechanical Translation between Japanese and English by Analogy Principle.**   
The paper that introduced translation by analogy, now called example-based machine translation. It is the basis of the adaptation step of the engine, which reuses the English of a similar stored sentence and replaces the changed words. 

**\[17\] Pallets. n.d. Flask Documentation.**   
The documentation of the Python web framework used for the application tier of the system. 

**\[18\] SQLite Consortium. n.d. About SQLite.**   
The description of the database engine used to store the accounts, the dictionary, the corpus, the history, and the audit log. 

**\[19\] Meta Open Source. n.d. React.**   
The home page of the JavaScript library used to build the browser interface of the system. 

**\[20\] MDN Web Docs. n.d. Web Speech API.**   
Documentation of the browser speech recognition interface that the mic button relies on. It states what the interface offers, and browser support varies; it does not show that the interface recognizes Bikol-Naga. 

**\[21\] Colin Percival and Simon Josefsson. 2016\.**   
The scrypt Password-Based Key Derivation Function. The specification of scrypt, the memory-hard function used to hash passwords in the system. 

**\[22\] OWASP Foundation. n.d. Authentication Cheat Sheet.**   
Guidance on password length, generic login error messages, and limiting failed attempts. It is the reference for the login behavior of the system and for the recommendation to raise the minimum password length from the demonstration value of 8 characters. 

**\[23\] OWASP Foundation. n.d. Password Storage Cheat Sheet.**   
Guidance on storing passwords as salted hashes and on the cost parameters of Argon2id and scrypt. It is the reference for the statement that the scrypt parameters used in the system are below the recommended minimum. 

**\[24\] OWASP Foundation. n.d. Logging Cheat Sheet.**  
Guidance on which security events to record. It is the reference for the events written to the audit log. 

**\[25\] Republic of the Philippines. 2012\. Republic Act No. 10173: Data Privacy Act of 2012\.**   
The law that governs the handling of personal data, cited for the handling of user data in the system.
